steps.title: Fungal diseases
steps.body: Powdery mildew, or oidium, covers leaves and berries with grey powder; it likes warm, shady conditions. Downy mildew, or peronospora, spreads in warm, wet weather. Botrytis bunch rot ruins grapes in wet harvests. All three came, or spread, in the 19th century. Sulphur sprays control powdery mildew; copper sprays, like Bordeaux mixture, control downy mildew.

steps.title: Pests and viruses
steps.body: Phylloxera attacks roots; grafting is the defence. Insects like grape moths damage berries and open the door to rot. Birds and wild boar eat ripe grapes. Viruses, like leafroll, spread through cuttings and insects; they reduce yield and delay ripening, and the only cure is replanting with clean material. Trunk diseases slowly kill old vines.
steps.highlight: Grafting for phylloxera; clean stock for viruses

steps.prompt: Match each problem to its main control.
steps.explanation: Each threat has its own defence.

steps.title: Integrated protection
steps.body: Modern growers combine methods: canopy management for airflow, resistant rootstocks, weather-based spraying only when risk is high, and natural predators. Pheromone traps confuse grape moths so they can't mate. New disease-resistant varieties, called PIWI, are being planted to cut spraying.

steps.explanation: Downy mildew needs warmth and moisture. Dry heat discourages it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Powdery and downy mildew and botrytis are the main fungal threats
Grafting stops phylloxera; clean stock limits viruses
Integrated protection combines canopy work, timing and natural tools
